GEOMORPHOLOGY PROCESS

  • Geomorphology is a scientific discipline, concerned with description and classification of earth's topographic features. All geomorphologic process occur due to two types of forces: Endogenic Forces (internal) and Exogenic Forces (external).
The study of distribution and movement of water, both in and below the earth surface as well as the impact of human activity on water availability and condition is known as Hydrology.

Endogenic Processes

  • These are geological processes that occur due to endogenic forces. All relief features on earth are subject to endogenic and exogenic forces. E.g.
  • Himalayas: They are continuously increasing (endogenic forces are significantly greater than exogenic forces).
  • Aravali: They are continuously decreasing (exogenic forces are significantly greater than endogenic forces).
  • Endogenic forces get their energy from within the earth (recall Convection Current Theory).

#### Effects of Endogenic Forces

  1. 1. Diastrophism: It is a process of deformation and movement of Earth's crust. These movements are responsible for shaping large-scale landforms over geological time periods.

Types of Diastrophism:

  • a) Orogenic Process: It is a process through which mountains are built.
  • b) Epeirogenic Process: It involves upliftment or warping of large parts of the Earth's crust.
  • c) Earthquake: It involves shaking of Earth.
  • d) Plate Tectonics: It explains how major landforms are created as a result of Earth's subterranean movements.
  1. 2. Volcanoes: They are commonly described as openings/vents where lava or magma erupts.

Exogenic Processes

  • These are geological processes that occur on the Earth's surface due to external forces (exogenic forces).
  • Denudation refers to long-term processes that cause the wearing away of earth's surface, leading to a reduction in elevation and relief of landforms and landscapes.
  • Exogenic agents are: Wind, glaciers, water (they are also termed as Denudation).
  • Source of energy for exogenic forces is the Sun.

Denudation Process: Process = Weathering + Mass Movements + Erosion/Transportation

  • Weathering — Breaking of rocks; driving force = Gravitational / Molecular stresses / Chemical actions.
  • Mass Movements — Weathering is not a pre-requisite but it aids the mass movement; driving force = Gravitational force.
  • Erosion/Transportation — Ex-situ process; agents = Wind, water; energy = Kinetic Energy.

Weathering

  • Weathering is the process of rocks and minerals breaking down or dissolving on the Earth's surface.

Types of Weathering

  1. 1. Physical Weathering: This involves the breakdown of rocks and soils through direct contact with atmospheric conditions, such as heat, water, ice, and pressure. E.g. Unloading and Expansion, Frost Wedging, Salt Crystallisation.
  2. 2. Chemical Weathering: This involves the decomposition of rocks and soils through chemical reactions, such as oxidation and reduction, carbonation, solution, and hydration.
  3. 3. Biological Weathering: It is also known as organic weathering, is the breakdown of rocks and soils through the activities of living organisms such as earthworms, rodents, etc.
Weathering is an in-situ process.

Effects of Weathering

  1. 1. Exfoliation: It is a process when large, curved plates, or slabs of rocks are stripped away from the outer surface of a rock mass.
  2. 2. Mass Movements: It is the downslope movement of soil, rock, and other debris under the influence of gravity. Gravity is not a prerequisite.

Types:

  1. 1. Rapid — Landslides (due to deforestation), avalanche, earthflow, mudflow (leads to soil liquefaction).
  2. 2. Slow: Creep (slow down slope movement of particles), solifluction (slow progressive movement of mass down a slope seen mainly in temperate regions).
  • Erosion: It involves transportation of rock debris through geomorphic agents like running water, groundwater, glaciers, winds and waves.

LANDFORMS

  • Landforms are natural or human-made features on the Earth's surface. They include hills, mountains, plains, and more. The landforms are formed due to various agents such as river, glaciers, wind, sea waves, groundwater, etc.

Types of Landforms

  1. 1. Erosional Landforms: They are created by the process of erosion.
  2. 2. Depositional Landforms: These are created when sediments are deposited in areas of reduced flow energy.

Landforms Created by River

  • A river goes through three stages: Youthful, mature, and old. The course of a river includes the upper stage, the middle stage, and the lower stage.
Youthful StageMature StageOld Stage
River flows in speed. E.g. V-shaped valley, Gorges, Canyon, Waterfalls, Entrenched meanderThe river flows through gradient to flat plain. E.g. MeandersThe final stage of river's journey. E.g. Ox-bow lakes, Delta, Flood plains
  • Erosional Landforms: Potholes (kettle-shaped depressions in the rocky beds of river valleys), Waterfalls, Plunge pools, V-shaped valley, Gorges, Canyons, River terraces, Entrenched meanders.
  • Depositional Landforms: Flood plains, ox-bow lakes (U-shaped lake that forms when a river's meander is cut off from the main river), Meanders, Alluvial fans, Levees, Braided channel, Alluvial fan.
Kabartal lake (Bihar) is Asia's largest ox-bow lake.

Landforms Created by Glaciers

  • Erosional Landforms: Cirque (they are created in heads of glacial valleys), Ridges / Arete, Horn, Hanging valleys, Glacial valleys.
  • Depositional Landforms: Moraines, Eskers, Drumlins (oval-shaped), Outwash plains.
Fjord: Sea water entering into the glacial valley. Tarn lakes: Created when water fills up in cirque.

Landforms Created by Groundwater (Karst Topography)

  • They are found in rocks that are permeable thinly bedded and highly jointed and cracked like limestone and dolomite, which are rich in calcium carbonate.
  • Erosional Landforms: Sink holes, Doline, Lapies, Uvalas, Limestone pavements.
  • Depositional Landforms: Stalactite, Pillars, Stalagmite.
  • Stalactite: Hanging from the ceiling.
  • Stalagmite: Rising from the ground.
  • Aquifer: Groundwater stored between layers of hard rock below the water table.

Landforms Created by Sea Waves

  • Erosional Landforms: Cliff, Caves, Stack, Arch.
  • Depositional Landforms: Beaches, Dunes, Bars, Barriers, Spits, Tombolo.

Landforms Created by Wind (Aeolian Landforms)

  • Erosional Landforms: Pediplain, Playas, Mushroom rock, Pedestal rocks.
  • Depositional Landforms: Sand dunes → Types: Barchan and Seif.
  • Oasis: Small patches of fertile land with water sources.

Loess

  • When the grains of sand are very fine and light, the wind can carry it over a very long distance, such sand gets deposited in large areas and is called as loess.
- Barchans: They are Crescent shaped dunes, whose points or wings are directed away from wind direction. They are found in Jaisalmer (Rajasthan).
- Seif: It is similar to a Barchan with only one wing.

Key concepts

  • Geomorphology — description and classification of Earth's topographic features. Two forces: Endogenic (internal) and Exogenic (external).
  • Hydrology = study of distribution and movement of water (in & below surface) and human impact on water availability/condition.
  • Endogenic processes — driven by Earth's internal energy (Convection Current Theory). Himalayas = increasing (endogenic > exogenic); Aravali = decreasing (exogenic > endogenic).
  • Effects of endogenic forces:
  • Diastrophism = deformation and movement of Earth's crust. Types: Orogenic (mountain building), Epeirogenic (upliftment/warping), Earthquake (shaking), Plate Tectonics (subterranean movements).
  • Volcanoes = openings/vents for lava/magma.
  • Exogenic processes — driven by the Sun. Agents: wind, glaciers, water (collectively = Denudation). Long-term wearing away of Earth's surface = Denudation. Denudation = Weathering + Mass Movements + Erosion/Transportation. Weathering needs gravitational/molecular/chemical actions; Mass movements use gravitational force; Erosion uses kinetic energy (wind, water).
  • Weathering = breaking down/dissolving rocks on Earth's surface (in-situ process). Types: Physical (heat, water, ice, pressure — e.g. unloading/expansion, frost wedging, salt crystallisation), Chemical (oxidation/reduction, carbonation, solution, hydration), Biological (organic — earthworms, rodents).
  • Effects of weathering: Exfoliation (curved plates/slabs stripped from rock surface); Mass movements (downslope, under gravity — Rapid: landslides, avalanche, earthflow, mudflow/soil liquefaction; Slow: creep, solifluction); Erosion (transport by water, groundwater, glaciers, wind, waves).
  • Landforms — natural or human-made features on Earth's surface. Types: Erosional (by erosion) and Depositional (when sediments settle in low-energy areas).
  • River landforms — three stages: Youthful (upper), Mature (middle), Old (lower).
  • Youthful: V-shaped valley, Gorges, Canyon, Waterfalls, Entrenched meander (fast flow).
  • Mature: Meanders (gradient to flat plain).
  • Old: Ox-bow lakes, Delta, Flood plains (final stage).
  • Erosional: Potholes, Waterfalls, Plunge pools, V-shaped valley, Gorges, Canyons, River terraces, Entrenched meanders.
  • Depositional: Flood plains, Ox-bow lakes (U-shaped; cut off from main river), Meanders, Alluvial fans, Levees, Braided channel.
  • Kabartal lake (Bihar) = Asia's largest ox-bow lake.
  • Glacier landforms:
  • Erosional: Cirque (heads of glacial valleys), Ridges/Arete, Horn, Hanging valleys, Glacial valleys.
  • Depositional: Moraines, Eskers, Drumlins (oval-shaped), Outwash plains.
  • Fjord = sea water entering glacial valley. Tarn lakes = water filling cirques.
  • Groundwater landforms (Karst topography) — in limestone/dolomite (rich in calcium carbonate), permeable, thin-bedded, jointed.
  • Erosional: Sink holes, Doline, Lapies, Uvalas, Limestone pavements.
  • Depositional: Stalactite (ceiling), Pillars, Stalagmite (ground). Aquifer = groundwater stored in hard rock below water table.
  • Sea-wave landforms:
  • Erosional: Cliff, Caves, Stack, Arch.
  • Depositional: Beaches, Dunes, Bars, Barriers, Spits, Tombolo.
  • Wind landforms (Aeolian):
  • Erosional: Pediplain, Playas, Mushroom rock, Pedestal rocks.
  • Depositional: Sand dunes — Types: Barchan (crescent, wings away from wind, found in Jaisalmer/Rajasthan) and Seif (Barchan with only one wing).
  • Oasis = small patches of fertile land with water.
  • Loess = very fine, light sand carried over long distances and deposited in large areas.
